subsection: 4. Economic and social challenges of the 1970s and 1980s: Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald

notes.h: Background: parties, the Troubles and EEC entry
notes.b: The leaders of the 1970s and 1980s worked within a fixed party system and faced two new pressures, conflict in the North and a changing economy. Three ideas recur in this period, so each is defined below.
points: Lynch became Taoiseach (prime minister) on 10 November 1966, after Seán Lemass resigned, and so inherited the economic boom of the 1960s.

Three parties dominated politics: Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and Labour. Fianna Fáil usually governed alone, so the alternative was a Fine Gael-Labour coalition (a government of two parties sharing power).
The Troubles (the conflict in Northern Ireland) began in 1968-69, which forced the Republic to decide how to respond to violence on its border.
Ireland, together with the United Kingdom, joined the EEC (the European Economic Community, the forerunner of the European Union) on 1 January 1973.
The balance of payments is the record of a country's dealings with the rest of the world. A deficit means more money flows out, for example to pay for imports, than flows in.

Liberalisation means relaxing legal or social controls, for example on contraception and divorce. Pluralism means a society of several groups and beliefs, which the state accommodates rather than favouring one.
The national debt is the total the state owes. It rose rapidly in these years because governments paid for spending by borrowing.
notes.tip: Exams on this period reward answers that tie each leader to specific actions and dates, so learn who held office when.

notes.b: The decade that began with EEC entry brought a series of external shocks that exposed the weaknesses of the Irish economy. Ireland was a small economy that depended on imports and exports, so what happened abroad hit it hard.
points: Ireland imported nearly all of its oil, so it was badly exposed when Arab oil producers (members of OPEC) cut supplies and raised prices after the Yom Kippur War of October 1973.
The oil price rise pushed up inflation (the general rise in prices) in the mid-1970s and ended the long post-war boom in Europe, which reduced demand for Irish exports.
The National Coalition of Fine Gael and Labour under Liam Cosgrave governed from March 1973 until 5 July 1977. It faced recession, rising unemployment and a large balance of payments deficit.
The Iranian Revolution of 1979 caused a second oil shock, raising fuel costs and prices again. Inflation reached about 20 per cent around 1981.
The European Monetary System (a scheme linking European currencies) began in March 1979. Ireland joined and Britain did not, so Ireland broke its link with sterling (the British pound) in 1979.

Governments responded to rising unemployment by raising public spending and borrowing, since the state hoped to protect jobs and services until growth returned. The national debt rose rapidly as a result.
By the early 1980s a large share of tax revenue was being spent on interest on the national debt, which left less money for services.
notes.tip: For the question on why the 1977 manifesto led to borrowing and a crisis, start from these shocks. The 1973-77 coalition was Cosgrave's, not Lynch's, so do not mix them up.

notes.b: Lynch succeeded Lemass and led Fianna Fáil through the first years of the Troubles, then returned to power in 1977. His career shows a leader who was stronger on external affairs than on the economy.
points: John Mary Lynch was born in Cork in 1917. He played hurling and football with Cork and won six All-Ireland medals in a row (1941-46: five in hurling, one in football), which made him famous; he qualified as a barrister and was first elected to the Dáil in 1948.
He was Minister for Education from 1957, for Industry and Commerce from 1959 and for Finance from 1965, and became Taoiseach on 10 November 1966 as a compromise choice between rival candidates.

He won the June 1969 general election with a majority of seats but lost the February 1973 election to the National Coalition of Fine Gael and Labour. He won again in June 1977 and was Taoiseach from 5 July 1977 to December 1979.

On 13 August 1969, after violence in Derry and Belfast, he said in a broadcast that the government could "no longer stand by". The army set up field hospitals near the border, but he ruled out sending troops across it.

His Northern policy was unity by consent and opposition to violence. He condemned internment (jailing without trial) when it began on 9 August 1971, and after Bloody Sunday on 30 January 1972 called a day of mourning and recalled the Irish ambassador from London.
After bombs in Dublin on 1 December 1972, so as to deal with the IRA, his government secured passage of the Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act to deal with the IRA.
He held Fianna Fáil together through the Arms Crisis, but was brought down by the economic position after 1977 and by the loss of two by-elections in 1979.

Strengths: he was popular and conciliatory, kept the party together and stopped the state being drawn into the conflict in the North. Weaknesses: critics said he was indecisive, slow to remove Haughey and Blaney, and that the 1977 programme he led was financially reckless.

Contemporaries admired his decency and moderate approach but doubted his firmness. Historians assess him as a skilful party manager and a moderating influence, whose record was stronger externally than internally and whose time was dominated by the North and the Arms Crisis.
notes.tip: Examiners ask how effective Lynch was, and you gain credit by separating external affairs (he kept the state out of the Northern conflict) from internal affairs (the Arms Crisis, the 1977 manifesto, borrowing) and ending on a verdict. For short answers, give dates and offices.

notes.b: The Arms Crisis was the most serious split in Fianna Fáil during the Troubles and tested Lynch's authority.
points: In April 1970 Special Branch (the police intelligence unit) told Lynch that senior ministers might be involved in a plan to import arms for Northern nationalists.
On 6 May 1970 Lynch dismissed Charles Haughey, Minister for Finance, and Neil Blaney, Minister for Agriculture. Kevin Boland resigned from the cabinet in protest.
Haughey, Blaney, Captain James Kelly of army intelligence, John Kelly from Belfast and the Belgian businessman Albert Luykx were charged with conspiracy to import arms illegally.
The case against Blaney was dropped before the trial, and Haughey and the other accused were acquitted in October 1970, so no one was convicted.
Haughey always maintained that the government had known about the plan, while Lynch's version was that he acted as soon as he had evidence. Historians still dispute who knew what.
The crisis left a lasting division between Lynch's supporters and Haughey's in Fianna Fáil, which continued into the 1980s, and it kept Haughey out of the cabinet for the years that followed.
notes.tip: If asked who was sacked in the Arms Crisis, name Haughey and Blaney, and say Boland resigned. Do not confuse this dismissal in 1970 with Haughey's becoming Taoiseach in 1979.

notes.h: The 1977 election and Lynch's second government
notes.b: Lynch returned to power in 1977 with a promise of more spending, and the consequences brought down his government within two and a half years.
points: Fianna Fáil's manifesto for the June 1977 general election promised to abolish domestic rates (a local tax on property) and car tax, and to create jobs by increasing spending.
The party won 84 of the 148 seats, then the largest majority in the history of the state. Lynch became Taoiseach on 5 July 1977.
The new government cut taxes and increased public spending, financed by borrowing, in the hope of lifting growth. This is why the current budget deficit and the national debt rose sharply.
Growth was strong at first, but inflation, a second oil crisis and the cost of the manifesto turned the position into a crisis by 1979.
Fianna Fáil lost two by-elections in Cork in November 1979, which weakened Lynch's authority, and he announced his resignation in December 1979.
Haughey defeated George Colley for the leadership of the party by 44 votes to 38 and became Taoiseach on 11 December 1979.
notes.tip: Exams ask why the manifesto led to borrowing and a crisis, and why Lynch resigned. Link the tax cuts and spending to borrowing, then the by-election defeats to his resignation. Colley was Haughey's rival; Lemass was his father-in-law.

notes.b: Haughey dominated Irish politics in the 1980s and divided opinion more than any other leader. He first warned that the country was overspending, then in 1987 made cuts that, with the Programme for National Recovery, helped prepare recovery.
points: Charles Haughey was born in 1925 in Castlebar, Co. Mayo, trained as an accountant, became very wealthy and married Maureen Lemass, a daughter of Seán Lemass.

He was Minister for Justice (1961-64), Agriculture (1964-66) and Finance (1966-70). Dismissed in the Arms Crisis, he rebuilt his support in the party in the 1970s, so he could return as Minister for Health and Social Welfare in 1977.
He was Taoiseach from 1979 to June 1981, from March to December 1982, and from March 1987 to 1992. His first term began on 11 December 1979 because he had defeated Colley for the leadership.
In a television address on 9 January 1980 he said the country was "living away beyond our means" and called for sacrifice. Yet his government's spending and borrowing continued to rise.

In 1987 he led a minority government (one without a majority of seats). Fine Gael under Alan Dukes promised not to oppose cuts if they stayed on course, the Tallaght Strategy of September 1987, so Minister for Finance Ray MacSharry could cut spending sharply.

The Programme for National Recovery, agreed in October 1987 by the government, trade unions, employers and farmers, held pay increases low in return for reducing the deficit, so workers accepted restraint in exchange for a firmer economy.
Strengths (which explain his loyal following): charisma, drive, loyalty from followers and a talent for tactics. Weaknesses: secrecy, extravagance and the use of power for personal advantage.

Contemporaries divided between those who saw a bold nationalist who got things done and those who saw a corrupting influence. Tribunals in the 1990s and 2000s later found he had received large sums from businessmen.
Historians judge him gifted but flawed: his record on the public finances was poor before 1987, but his later cuts and the PNR helped prepare recovery.
notes.tip: Examiners credit the 1980 address and the 1987 programme with dates, and explicit strengths and weaknesses. Do not mix up the Tallaght Strategy, which was Fine Gael's support for cuts, with the Programme for National Recovery, which was an agreement with the social partners.

notes.b: Three general elections in eighteen months (June 1981, February 1982 and November 1982) produced weak governments and a sense of crisis. The reason was that no party or coalition held a secure majority.
points: The June 1981 election produced a Fine Gael-Labour coalition under Garret FitzGerald, which depended on the votes of independent TDs.
That government fell in January 1982 when its budget, which proposed VAT on children's clothes and shoes, was defeated. A new election followed in February 1982.
Haughey returned as Taoiseach in March 1982 with the support of the Workers' Party, some independents and Tony Gregory, who won investment for inner-city Dublin in return.

In 1982 a series of scandals followed: phone-tapping of journalists, a leadership challenge against Haughey in October, and on 14 August the arrest of the murderer Malcolm MacArthur in the apartment of the Attorney General, Patrick Connolly.

The phrase "grotesque, unbelievable, bizarre and unprecedented" was applied to these events. Conor Cruise O'Brien turned it into the acronym GUBU, which became shorthand for the political culture of the time.
Haughey's government fell in November 1982 when the Workers' Party and Tony Gregory withdrew their support, and FitzGerald returned as Taoiseach in December 1982.
notes.tip: If asked why there were three elections in eighteen months, explain that minority governments depended on small groups: the January 1982 budget defeat and the November 1982 loss of support ended two of them. For GUBU, note that the phrase was applied to the events and O'Brien coined the acronym.

notes.b: FitzGerald, an economist and Fine Gael leader, headed two coalitions with Labour and tried to modernise the state. He is remembered for his vision of a more tolerant Ireland more than for his economic results.
points: Garret FitzGerald was born in 1926, the son of Desmond FitzGerald, a minister in the first Free State government. He worked as an economist and lecturer before becoming Minister for Foreign Affairs from 1973 to 1977.
He became leader of Fine Gael in 1977 and was Taoiseach from June 1981 to March 1982 and from December 1982 to March 1987.

In 1981 he announced a constitutional crusade to make the Republic more pluralist, with divorce reform and fewer Catholic influences on the law. The aim was to make it more attractive to Northern unionists.
The crusade had limited results. The 1983 referendum inserted the Eighth Amendment, which FitzGerald had reservations about in that wording, and the 1986 divorce referendum was defeated.
In 1985 his government liberalised the law on contraceptives (the Health (Family Planning) (Amendment) Act), allowing non-medical contraceptives to be sold without prescription to people over 18.
He set up the New Ireland Forum in 1983 and signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with Margaret Thatcher on 15 November 1985.
His economic record was weak: his coalition tried to reduce the deficit but unemployment and the debt kept rising, and Labour left the government in January 1987 over spending cuts.
Strengths: intellect, integrity and a vision of a modern, tolerant Ireland. Weaknesses: a tendency to overreach and difficulty holding a coalition together on economic policy.
Contemporaries admired his honesty and energy but saw him as unworldly. Historians credit him with opening Irish politics to new ideas but judge his economic record the weakest part.
notes.tip: Examiners credit named actions with dates: the 1981 crusade, the 1985 contraception law and the referendums. Remember FitzGerald's two terms (1981-82 and 1982-87) were separated by Haughey's short 1982 government. The Forum (1983-84) was a report; the Agreement (1985) was a treaty.

notes.h: Referendums of 1983 and 1986 and the pluralism debate
notes.b: FitzGerald hoped to liberalise the Constitution, but two referendums showed how far public opinion still lagged behind. Comparing them shows how limited pluralism remained.
points: The Eighth Amendment, approved on 7 September 1983 by about two to one, acknowledged the right to life of the unborn, with due regard to the equal right to life of the mother.
It was backed by anti-abortion campaigners, and FitzGerald had reservations about the wording, so it was not simply his own policy.
The divorce referendum of 26 June 1986 sought to remove the constitutional ban on divorce and was defeated by about two to one.
The results showed that the church still had great influence over social questions in the 1980s, and that liberalisation had not progressed as FitzGerald had hoped.
Debates about pluralism and the Constitution in the 1980s are an important background to the changes of the 1990s.
notes.tip: Short answers ask what the 1983 and 1986 referendums decided: the Eighth Amendment was passed, and the divorce referendum was defeated. For what the results showed, say that they revealed the church's continuing influence over social questions. Use the exact wording of the amendment given here.

notes.b: The economic problems of the early 1980s hit ordinary people directly through jobs, emigration and taxes. The public finances eventually forced a change of direction.
points: Unemployment rose from about 7 per cent in 1979 to over 15 per cent by the mid-1980s, and the live register (the list of people claiming unemployment payments) reached about a quarter of a million by 1987.

Emigration returned on a large scale, as jobs were scarce, with about 200,000 more people leaving than arriving over the decade. Many were well-educated young people heading for Britain, the United States and continental Europe.
The national debt passed 100 per cent of national income by 1987, and interest payments absorbed a large part of tax revenue.
Tax rates rose to pay for services, which discouraged investment and made the burden on workers heavy.
Cuts in spending in 1987 and the PNR brought the deficit down, which laid the base for the recovery of the 1990s.
notes.tip: Keep the economic record apart from the political record in your answers. Use only the figures given here, and say "about" for emigration.

notes.h: Assessment: the leadership of the 1970s and 1980s
notes.b: Judging these leaders means weighing what each achieved against what each left undone. The best answers pair successes with limits and contemporary views with later ones.
points: Lynch: success in keeping the state out of the Northern conflict and holding the party together, but a limit in leaving the economy in difficulty after 1977 because the 1977 programme relied on borrowing.
Haughey: success in presiding over a turn towards financial discipline in 1987, but a limit in his earlier government, which was marked by deficits and scandal, such as GUBU.
FitzGerald: success in putting pluralism and the Northern question on the agenda, but a limit in being unable to deliver social change in referendums or economic recovery.
Contemporary view: voters repeatedly turned governments out, partly because each had to impose or defend painful measures.

Later view: historians describe the 1980s as a lost decade for growth, though they see the late 1980s as the beginning of recovery. They debate how far credit belongs to Haughey, MacSharry, Dukes and the European funds.
notes.tip: For the 100-mark essay on how well governments coped, give a clear judgement with balanced points on economic shocks, political instability, the North and social issues. Tie each leader to specific actions and dates, and pair contemporary with later views.

keyTerms.definition: The record of a country's trade and financial dealings with the rest of the world; a deficit means more money leaves than enters.
The relaxation of legal or social controls, for example on contraception, divorce or censorship.
The principle that a society contains several different groups and beliefs, and that the state should accommodate them rather than favour one.
The 1970 crisis in which Lynch dismissed Haughey and Blaney over a plan to import arms for Northern nationalists.
An acronym, from Conor Cruise O'Brien, for the 1982 scandals, taken from the description grotesque, unbelievable, bizarre and unprecedented.
The 1983 to 1984 forum of nationalist parties from the Republic and the SDLP that reported on possible futures for Ireland.
The October 1987 agreement between government, unions, employers and farmers on pay restraint and a reduction in the deficit.
Fine Gael leader Alan Dukes's decision in 1987 not to oppose the government's budget cuts so long as they continued.
The total amount owed by the state, which rose rapidly in the late 1970s and 1980s as the government borrowed to fund services.
The 1983 constitutional amendment recognising the equal right to life of the unborn.
